text: A web-based application for stadium safety workflows
Supriyo Hara   •   Astha Singh   •   Tushar Mondal

Good morning. We are Team EUREKA: Supriyo Hara, Astha Singh and Tushar Mondal. Our project is PULSE, a web-based application for crowd monitoring and incident review. We created it to help an operator identify local crowd bottlenecks and inspect relevant incidents in a common interface. We demonstrate the workflow with synthetic stadium data. Our current work is a prototype, and we are not claiming proven crowd-safety outcomes. The exact problem is local crowd congestion: one gate or corridor can become overloaded even while other parts of a venue have spare space. Staff need to identify the hotspot and connect it with incident information quickly. Existing measures include stewards, CCTV and radio communication. Our design hypothesis is that bringing the information into one browser view can reduce the effort of switching between separate views. We have not surveyed operators or proved a gap in all commercial systems. Without a shared view, an operator must still reconcile the information manually. MetLife's official stadium description gives a capacity of 82,500, illustrating the scale of the setting, not the number of PULSE users. HSE guidance calls for monitoring both total numbers and the distribution of people. Sources: https://www.metlifestadium.com/stadium/about-metlife-stadium; https://www.hse.gov.uk/event-safety/crowd-management-monitoring.htm. PULSE brings crowd-zone indicators and incident details together so an operator can review where attention is needed. Consider the seeded demonstration values: Gate A is 92%, Gate B 61%, Gate C 34%, Gate D 22%. These are normalized synthetic crowd scores in data.js. They are not sensor measurements or calibrated physical occupancy. Gate D is labelled a VIP entry, so a lower score alone does not mean staff may redirect everyone there. A real decision also requires access permissions, route capacity and staff verification. The concept flow ends in an operator choosing a response; it does not mean the prototype contacts emergency services. Routing uses prewritten options. The application is plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript, with Three.js for visual effects. It runs in the browser and is hosted as static content. Seeded data.js values feed rule-based risk labels, heuristic triage and prewritten routes. Webcam frames can be analysed by the pre-trained TensorFlow.js COCO-SSD detector, returning object classes, confidence values and bounding boxes. This is the real computer-vision component; the code does not load YOLOv8. Open-Meteo supplies temperature and humidity for fixed MetLife coordinates. An external LLM can provide chat and advice through OpenRouter or an alternate Anthropic path. The weather request and LLM calls require internet. State is held in JavaScript and some data in localStorage. No shared database, secure backend, real authentication or validated multi-user dispatch is implemented. Our contribution: a combined operator workflow

Contribution is integration. No new AI algorithm or proven market-first claim.
Camera weapon labels are proxies. Age/gender labels and alert locations are synthetic.

Our contribution is an integrated demonstration workflow: crowd indicators, object-detection experiments and incident review in one browser application. Compared with viewing CCTV alone, the interface adds location context and a structured incident view. This is an integration contribution, not a claim that no commercial product does this or that we invented a new AI algorithm. COCO-SSD is a pre-trained neural object detector. It detects people and common objects. Crowd labels and incident urgency are deterministic rules. The 30-minute crowd forecast uses a multiplier based on match time, not a trained predictive model. Routes are selected from prewritten options, not calculated with a live graph algorithm. Current camera code maps phones and other ordinary objects to weapon labels, uses random locations and derives age/gender display values from bounding-box coordinates. Those are demo artifacts, not valid recognition results. Do not demonstrate these labels as accurate security or demographic inference. A student demonstration can run on a laptop with a modern browser, static hosting and, optionally, a webcam. TensorFlow.js and the pre-trained detector are open-source tools. External API usage remains subject to provider terms and limits; there is no evidence of a completely cost-free production service. The static interface can be distributed to more users, but sessions do not share live incident state and detection performance depends on the client device. For operational scaling, add a secure backend, role-based access, a shared database, real sensor ingestion, calibrated crowd estimates and human-approved response procedures. During this review, demo sign-in and Ops rendering were exercised locally. The crowd canvas raised a malformed colour error and needs a fix before a live demonstration. Three repository tests passed, but they test duplicated helper examples rather than executing the app. Evidence supports an early laboratory prototype. A formal TRL-4 claim needs documented component validation in a laboratory, which the repository does not establish. Staff identify hotspots with less effort. Fans receive clearer
guidance after staff verify the situation.
Hotspot-identification time, response-selection time and missed alerts.
Outcome improvements have not yet been measured.

The intended benefit for staff is less time spent finding a congested zone and reviewing related incidents. Fans could benefit indirectly from clearer guidance after staff verification, while accessible route options support consideration of mobility needs. We have no field evidence of reduced injuries, shorter queues or lower cost. The quantitative evidence on this slide is prototype scope: eight seeded crowd zones, three prewritten route options and emergency phrase data in twelve languages. These figures are not operational outcomes. A pilot should compare operators using a manual scenario table against operators using PULSE on equivalent synthetic incidents. Measure median time to identify the highest-risk zone, time to select an appropriate response, missed incidents and false alarms. Later test camera counts against annotated ground truth. Only after collecting the baseline and app results should we calculate percentage improvement.
